keptItems.title: A Peaceful Detective Mystery to Watch
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. keptItems.title: My Weekend at Adult Summer Camp
keptItems.summaryEvidence: A t Camp Social , where grown women return to girlhood, friendship has no preamble. Within 15 minutes of meeting eight of the campers from Cabin 3, I learned this: In their 50s and 60s, they have no use for the menstrual discs in the camp swag bag; one of them found online dating so depressing after her divorce that she’s given up entirely; when they laugh, they pee a little; they feel like they’ve known one another for years, even though most of them met last night. The campers signed up for this weekend-long adult summer camp for exactly this purpose—to make new friends. On August 21, more than 400 women, some as young as 21, some older than 80, arrived at what usually is a children’s sleepaway camp in the Poconos to spend the weekend bunking in twin beds in log cabins, climbing the ropes course, developing middle-school-level inside jokes, making friendship bracelets, and performing choreographed dances at the flagpole to Cher’s “Believe” and Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” Everyone at Camp Social, regardless of age, is referred to as a “girl.” The camp promises to recreate a childhood experience so that grown-ups can bond with one another as easily as they might have as kids. keptItems.title: El Niño Has Become a Doom Loop
keptItems.summaryEvidence: In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, along the equator, scientists have drawn a box. It’s a big box, two-thirds the size of China, yet hardly anyone lives inside it. This rectangular swath of open ocean is monitored by satellites and a network of moored buoys that measure minute changes in the temperature of the water, with an eye toward anomalies. Every few years or so, driven by changing winds and currents, the water temperature in this part of the ocean starts to rise; even a half degree Celsius above normal over months warrants a designation that an El Niño phase has begun. That’s enough warming to unleash floods and fires, drought and famine, around the world. The box is called Niño 3.4. Right now, it’s hot in the box. “Like a baby pool,” Kristina Tietjen, who spent most of August scuba diving in the middle of this mass of abnormally warm water, told me. Tietjen has been coming to the world’s largest atoll, Kiritimati, for more than a decade to study its coral reefs. She usually dives in a medium-weight wetsuit; this trip, her team needed only rash guards. It is still early in this El Niño cycle—which is likely to be the strongest ever recorded—but the waters around Kiritimati have already been 3 to 4 degrees Celsius above normal. Tietjen’s time on Kiritimati (pronounced like Christmas ) has allowed her to watch, in brutal detail, what these repeated warm-water cycles, playing out in a steadily warming ocean, mean for the great tropical coral reefs here, which were once near pristine. During her first El Niño, in 2015–16, 90 percent of Kiritimati’s coral reef died. Year
